passages.t: Twelve monthly divisions, and the leaders of the tribes
passages.happening:
The army is listed in twelve divisions, each serving one month of the year, ‘There were 24,000 men in each division’ (verse 1). Each month has its commander (verses 2-15), among them ‘Joab’s brother Asahel, and his son Zebadiah was commander after him’ (verse 7).

Then come the leaders of the tribes (verses 16-22), among them ‘over Benjamin was Jaasiel son of Abner’ (verse 21). ‘David did not count the men aged twenty or under, because the LORD had said that He would make Israel as numerous as the stars of the sky’ (verse 23). ‘Joab son of Zeruiah began to count the men but did not finish. For because of this census wrath came upon Israel, and the number was not entered in the Book of the Chronicles of King David’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 23 to 27 are a long pause in David's last years, showing the kingdom put in order before Solomon takes the throne. After the temple's people, this chapter turns to the rest of the realm. David hands over not only a building plan but a working kingdom. Who to notice: the commanders who were David's mighty men, and Jaasiel son of Abner.

The army was a rotating citizen militia. Each division served one month a year and then went home to its farms and flocks, which spread the burden and kept a trained force always on hand. Many scholars note that the Hebrew word for thousand, eleph, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so 24,000 may count units rather than men; others take the figures as plain totals. The question touches the size of the army, not the meaning of the list. The word for division, machaloqet, is the same word used for the courses of priests and Levites: army and temple alike serve in ordered turns.

Most of the twelve commanders also appear among David's mighty men in chapter 11 and 2 Samuel 23, the veterans of his wars given charge in the settled kingdom. Asahel was killed by Abner early in David's reign, and his son commands after him. Jaasiel son of Abner was likely the son of Saul's old commander, a sign that David brought Saul's house into his government. The tribal list leaves out Gad and Asher and counts Aaron and the halves of Manasseh separately.

Verses 23 and 24 break the pattern to remember the census of chapter 21. David had not counted the young men, trusting the promise to Abraham, and the count Joab began was never finished or written into the royal records.
passages.later: God's promise to Abraham was, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able” (Genesis 15:5), and then, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5).
passages.asks: Twelve divisions each took their month and went home. Ask whether you carry your share of the work, or leave it to the same few. And ask what God has promised to multiply that you keep trying to count.

passages.happening:
Officials oversee the king's storehouses in the capital and in the country, the farm workers, the vineyards and their wine, the olive and sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah, the stores of oil, the herds in Sharon and in the valleys, the camels and the flocks (verses 25-31).

David's uncle Jonathan advises the king, ‘he was a man of insight and a scribe’ (verse 32). Ahithophel is the king's adviser, and ‘Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend’ (verse 33). Ahithophel is followed by Jehoiada and Abiathar, and Joab commands the army (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The royal economy shows how an ancient king lived: storehouses, fields, vineyards, olive and sycamore-fig groves in the Shephelah, the low hills between the coastal plain and the highlands of Judah, and herds on the plain of Sharon. Two of the stewards were foreigners, Obil the Ishmaelite over the camels and Jaziz the Hagrite over the flocks, men from desert peoples who knew those animals best.

The last names carry a story the reader of Samuel knows. Ahithophel, the king's counselor, later joined Absalom's revolt, and Hushai, the king's friend, defeated his advice and stayed loyal. The king's friend, re'a, was probably a recognized court position, a trusted confidant. The Chronicler does not tell the revolt, but he records that others succeeded Ahithophel.

Lists like these were the stuff of royal archives, and verse 24 names one, the Book of the Chronicles of King David. With the realm in order, chapter 28 can open with David calling all these officials to Jerusalem.
passages.later: Second Samuel says that ‘in those days the advice of Ahithophel was like the consultation of the word of God’ (2 Samuel 16:23), before he turned against the king.
passages.asks: Ahithophel was the wisest counselor and the one who turned; Hushai was the friend who stayed. Ask whom you trust for counsel, and whether they are also your friend. And ask whether you are the kind of friend who stays when others leave.
